summary: Children generate their own measurement data by measuring several real objects to the nearest whole unit, then display the data on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there); height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. Teaching works best when children measure first, then build the plot, with a ruler kept physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt. A line may be pre-scaled as an early scaffold, but constructing the scale on a plain line is the fuller skill the objective targets. A tally or frequency table can bridge from raw measurements, but the axis is an ordered measurement scale, not the reorderable categories of earlier tally/category charts. Core activity: a measure-and-plot build (hands-on or on-screen). Supporting activities: interpreting a given plot, and a reference/reveal of a finished plot for the meaning of each X and position.
misconceptions: Reading the height of a stack as the length ('the tallest stack is the longest object')
Drawing only the values that occurred and spacing them evenly, so a value with no data is omitted and the intervals become unequal
Measuring from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every length is off by a unit
Treating each X as one unit of length rather than one object

activities.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
steps: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
activities.insight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.

activities.title: Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
steps: Study a completed line plot and answer count questions such as 'How many objects were 6 cm long?' by counting the Xs in a stack.
Answer position questions such as 'How long is the longest object?' by reading the scale, not the stack height.
Explain what an empty whole-number value on the scale means (no object had that length).
Predict what changes if one more object measuring 6 cm were added (one more X on the 6 stack; the position is unchanged).
activities.insight: Reading a line plot means deliberately choosing between counting (height) and reading position (length); the same plot answers both kinds of question in different ways.

activities.title: Reference reveal: what each X and each position means
steps: Point to (or tap) a stack and state 'how many' objects it represents.
Point to (or tap) a position on the scale and state 'how long' that is.
Use the finished plot as a reference while checking a plot you built yourself.
activities.insight: Each X stands for one object, placed at its measured length; a stack's height is a count, its position is a length.

checkQuestion: Give the child a ruler and 6-8 small objects. Say: 'Measure each of these to the nearest whole centimetre, then show all your measurements on this line.' Provide a plain, unmarked horizontal line. Watch how they scale the axis, place the Xs, handle two objects that share a length, and handle a value in the range that nothing measured.
checkAnswer: Marks the horizontal axis in equal whole-unit intervals spanning the full range INCLUDING values with no data; measures each object from zero; stacks exactly one X per object at its measured value (two same-length objects give a stack of two); can then read 'how many' by counting Xs and 'how long' by reading position.
